\section[capotar]{capotar — to overturn, to flip over}

\label{lesson:PT-C300-capotar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to collide, then the Portuguese for the mishap.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: capotar}
\textbf{capotar} — \textquotedblleft{}to overturn, to flip over\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O carro capotou duas vezes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The car flipped over twice.}
\end{quote}

Of cars and other vehicles.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{capotar} is usually traced to French \emph{capoter} \textquotedblleft{}to overturn\textquotedblright{}; EtymDB has no entry, and the origin is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{capotar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{capotar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{capotar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to collide, then the Portuguese for the mishap, then say \emph{capotar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does capotar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To overturn, to flip over\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[a travagem]{a travagem — the braking}

\label{lesson:PT-C300-travagem}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the mishap, then the Portuguese for to overturn.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a travagem}
\textbf{a travagem} — \textquotedblleft{}the braking\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ouvimos uma travagem e depois um barulho enorme.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We heard someone brake hard and then a huge bang.}
\end{quote}

European Portuguese; in Brazil, \emph{a freada}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{travagem} is built on \emph{travar} \textquotedblleft{}to brake, to hold back\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{trave} \textquotedblleft{}a beam\textquotedblright{}, which comes from Latin \emph{trabs} \textquotedblleft{}a beam\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a travagem}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a travagem}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the mishap, then the Portuguese for to overturn, then say \emph{a travagem} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[os danos]{os danos — the damage}

\label{lesson:PT-C300-danos}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to overturn, then the Portuguese for the braking.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: os danos}
\textbf{os danos} — \textquotedblleft{}the damage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Os danos no carro foram grandes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The damage to the car was serious.}
\end{quote}

Usually plural. \emph{Danos materiais} — damage to property.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dano} is inherited from Latin \emph{damnum} \textquotedblleft{}loss, damage\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[danificar]{danificar — to damage}

\label{lesson:PT-C300-danificar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the braking, then the Portuguese for the damage.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: danificar}
\textbf{danificar} — \textquotedblleft{}to damage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A chuva danificou o telhado.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The rain damaged the roof.}
\end{quote}

Formal; in speech, \emph{estragar}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{danificar} is a learned word from Late Latin \emph{damnificāre} \textquotedblleft{}to injure\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{damnum} \textquotedblleft{}loss\textquotedblright{} and \emph{facere} \textquotedblleft{}to make\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[o estrago]{o estrago — the harm, the mess; the ruin}

\label{lesson:PT-C300-estrago}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the damage, then the Portuguese for to damage.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o estrago}
\textbf{o estrago} — \textquotedblleft{}the harm, the mess; the ruin\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O estrago na cozinha foi enorme.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The mess in the kitchen was huge.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{estragar}, ‘to spoil’. \emph{Fazer estragos} — to do damage.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{estrago} is built on \emph{estragar} \textquotedblleft{}to spoil\textquotedblright{}, which is usually traced to Vulgar Latin \emph{stragāre}, from Latin \emph{strāgēs} \textquotedblleft{}destruction\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[(dialogue)]{Revisão dos capítulos 293–300}

\begin{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the officer, the patrol, to patrol, to keep watch over, surveillance
  \item the investigation, to investigate, the inspector, the detective, the clue
  \item the suspect, the suspicion, to arrest, the arrest, the person arrested
  \item the handcuffs, to handcuff, to catch, the prisoner, the cell
  \item the tip-off, the statement, the testimony, to sentence, to acquit
  \item the verdict, to appeal, the appeal, the inmate, to set free
  \item the accident, the crash, to crash, to collide, the mishap
  \item to overturn, the braking, the damage, to damage, the harm

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The officer? (\textbf{o agente}.) The patrol? (\textbf{a patrulha}.) To patrol? (\textbf{patrulhar}.) To keep watch over? (\textbf{vigiar}.) Surveillance? (\textbf{a vigilância}.) The investigation? (\textbf{a investigação}.) To investigate? (\textbf{investigar}.) The inspector? (\textbf{o inspetor}.) The detective? (\textbf{o detetive}.) The clue? (\textbf{o indício}.) The suspect? (\textbf{o suspeito}.) The suspicion? (\textbf{a suspeita}.) To arrest? (\textbf{deter}.) The arrest? (\textbf{a detenção}.) The person arrested? (\textbf{o detido}.) The handcuffs? (\textbf{as algemas}.) To handcuff? (\textbf{algemar}.) To catch? (\textbf{prender}.) The prisoner? (\textbf{o preso}.) The cell? (\textbf{a cela}.) The tip-off? (\textbf{a denúncia}.) The statement? (\textbf{o depoimento}.) The testimony? (\textbf{o testemunho}.) To sentence? (\textbf{condenar}.) To acquit? (\textbf{absolver}.) The verdict? (\textbf{o veredicto}.) To appeal? (\textbf{recorrer}.) The appeal? (\textbf{o recurso}.) The inmate? (\textbf{o recluso}.) To set free? (\textbf{libertar}.) The accident? (\textbf{o acidente}.) The crash? (\textbf{o choque}.) To crash? (\textbf{chocar}.) To collide? (\textbf{colidir}.) The mishap? (\textbf{o sinistro}.) To overturn? (\textbf{capotar}.) The braking? (\textbf{a travagem}.) The damage? (\textbf{os danos}.) To damage? (\textbf{danificar}.) The harm? (\textbf{o estrago}.)
